How and why taxonAlign was built

Source: vignettes/development-history.qmd

This document is not a tutorial – Get started is that. It’s a record of why taxonAlign exists and the real, messy invertebrate names that shaped its design. Every number and example name below is real, drawn from actually running this package against real data during its development.

The package has since been split in two (issue #26): taxonAlign now does the matching and updating, and the functions that build a reference (generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list(), load_NSL(), …) live in the companion package taxonAlign.dataprep. The AFD export used below, the AFD’s own CSV format, has since been superseded by its National Species List format, released as load_taxonomic_resources("NSL_animals"); the reader for the CSV format, load_AFD(), now lives only in taxonAlign.dataprep’s AFD-data-processing vignette, for comparisons between the two. The AFD and iNaturalist exports aren’t distributed with either package; point the paths at your own copies to run the code, substituting in the invertebrate database’s taxon list with one from your project.

Why this package exists

An Australian invertebrates trait database assembled trait data from hundreds of source datasets, each identifying its specimens in its own way – a perfect example that invertebrate taxonomy is, in practice, far messier than “Genus species”. Real names from that database include things like:

  • "Genus 1 sp.01 Corinnidae" – a museum voucher/morphospecies code: unidentified to genus, with the family recorded separately.
  • "Lasioglossum (Parasphecodes)" – the zoological Genus (Subgenus) bracket convention, rarely written by taxonomists working in plants (where taxonAlign’s design lineage, APCalign, comes from).
  • "Themognatha affinis affinis" – a tautonymous subspecies (the nominotypical subspecies repeats its species epithet)

Aligning tens of thousands of names like these against an accepted taxonomy, by hand, doesn’t scale. The tool originally built to do this was a bespoke internal script, using ideas drawn from APCalign: it read one hard-coded combination of taxonomic references (the Australian Faunal Directory, AFD, supplemented by an iNaturalist export for names AFD didn’t cover) and ran a fixed sequence of match attempts against them.

taxonAlign generalises that script’s ideas into a reusable package: the reference is supplied by the user (their own table, a known source, or a live GBIF fetch – any mix of these), and the matching engine handles every taxonomic rank present in that reference, reflecting both the inability of researchers to identify some taxa to species – or even genus – and that some trait values are applicable across all species in a broader taxon grouping.

Building the reference: AFD + iNaturalist

load_AFD() (see above) reads and reshapes the real, ~117,000-row AFD export into taxonAlign’s flat schema.

library(taxonAlign)

afd <- load_AFD("AFD.csv")
nrow(afd)
#> [1] 310050

AFD’s coverage isn’t uniform across invertebrate phyla – it’s comprehensive for some well-studied groups (insects especially) but considerably less complete for others, so it alone doesn’t cover every name a broad invertebrate database needs. The original workflow supplemented it with an export of iNaturalist’s Australian invertebrate taxonomy. taxonAlign has no built-in iNaturalist loader (unlike AFD and APC, iNaturalist has no single canonical export shape worth building a permanent loader around), so this reshaping step is written out directly:

inat_raw <- readr::read_csv("iNat_inverts_in_Australia.csv")

inat <- inat_raw |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    canonical_name = scientificName, scientific_name = scientificName, taxon_rank = taxonRank,
    taxonomic_status = "accepted", taxonomic_dataset = "iNat", genus = genus,
    taxon_ID = taxonID, accepted_name_usage_ID = taxonID
  )
nrow(inat)
#> [1] 54926

Note taxonomic_status is hardcoded to "accepted" for every row – this export carries no synonym information at all, so iNaturalist can widen genus/species coverage beyond AFD but can never help resolve a name that’s a synonym of something else the way AFD’s own synonym data can.

prepare_taxonomic_resources() combines the two into the single, rank-split, priority-ordered structure align_taxa()/update_taxa() expect. Listing AFD first means it is listed as the taxonomic reference whenever a name is present in both:

resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(list(AFD = afd, iNat = inat))
names(resources)
#> [1] "species" "genus" "subgenus" "subgenus_v2" "complex" "hybrid" ... "family" ... "order" ...

Aligning a real invertebrate name list

The Australian invertebrates database keeps its own record of every raw name it has ever needed to align, and what it was resolved to – in two separate columns. taxon_name records the species-level resolution only, and is deliberately left blank whenever a name was correctly resolved to a higher rank instead (“exception flag” rather than a failure). aligned_name records the resolution at every rank, including the higher-rank cases taxon_name leaves blank, in the same bracketed "Genus sp. [original; identifier]" format used throughout this package. Both are used below – taxon_name for the species-level comparison, aligned_name for the higher-rank one. At the time of writing, this list holds 5,154 distinct (name, source dataset) pairs.

old <- readr::read_csv("your_own_copy_of_the_name_list.csv")
nrow(old)
#> [1] 5154

updated <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(
  old$original_name, resources,
  identifier = old$dataset_id, # source dataset becomes identified in []
  hybrids = TRUE, 
  intergrades_affinis = TRUE,
  consider_english_name_endings = TRUE, # automatically replace English name endings with Latin ones
  include_bracketed_info = TRUE, # retain notes and original names in []
  progress = TRUE # toolbar to show progress
)

hybrids/intergrades_affinis opt in to recognising naming conventions that can only ever resolve to genus rank (a hybrid formula, an intergrade, a collector’s indecision between two taxa, a graded/ “affinis”/“cf.” identification); consider_english_name_endings opts in to recognising an informal vernacular ending ("Coccinellid" for family Coccinellidae) and trying an exact match on the formal Latin equivalent before falling back to fuzzy matching.

How well does it work?

The database’s historical file records two things worth comparing separately: taxon_name (species only) and aligned_name (every rank, in the exact "Genus sp. [original; identifier]" bracketed format include_bracketed_info = TRUE reproduces).

comparison <- old |>
  dplyr::select(original_name, taxon_name, old_aligned_name = aligned_name) |>
  dplyr::bind_cols(updated |> dplyr::select(new_aligned_name = aligned_name))

Species-level (2,873 rows where taxon_name is filled in): 2,861 (99.6%) match exactly. Only 12 disagree, and each one is informative rather than a package bug: six are species genuinely absent from both AFD and iNaturalist (the pipeline conservatively stops at genus rather than guessing – including one, "Euastacus coughrani", absent from both); two are likely fuzzy-matching imprecision within Euastacus, a genus of dozens of very similarly-epithet-ed crayfish species, that reflects the limits of fuzzy matching, especially with incomplete resources and typos in submitted names; two are "Onthophagus bulga" matched identically both times but recorded inconsistently in the historical file itself; one, "Incertae Sedis", resolves to AFD’s own literal “position uncertain” placeholder rather than the more specific subfamily a human curator assigned from context; and the last, "Themognatha affinis affinis", was a real bug – a tautonymous subspecies textually indistinguishable from an affinity hedge, fixed by checking for a real, resource-verified exact match before ever falling back to the “uncertain identification” reading.

Higher-rank (the other 2,281 rows): matching the exact bracketed string is a stricter bar here – format-sensitive in a way species names aren’t – and it shows: 1,911 (87.1%) match exactly. That’s a real drop from the species-level number, but the same two resource combinations agree with each other on 98.5% of this subset, which suggests most of the gap is disagreement with the (older) historical file, reflecting improvements in matching algorithms since this package was developed and the original code was upgraded.

What real invertebrate names taught the matching engine

Several of match_taxa()’s ~20 sequential match blocks exist specifically because of patterns noted during test runs with the invertebrate dataset, but not anticipated in advance:

  • The bracketed subgenus convention needed its own dedicated match blocks – a plain string-cleaning pass (borrowed from APCalign, which never has to handle this convention) strips the parentheses but keeps the bracketed word, which can otherwise be mistaken for a species epithet and fuzzy-matched to an unrelated real species (issue #14).

  • Fuzzy matching a higher rank needed to search broadest-first, not most-specific-first – checked directly against the real name list: 52% of names that fuzzy-matched a higher rank also fuzzy-matched a real candidate at a different rank, mostly not coincidence but a systematic pattern – an informal vernacular adjective ("Coccinellid") must be assumed to signal the broadest group the name might refer to, not a specific genus (issue #12), unless additional information is available.

  • consider_english_name_endings (the other half of issue #12) recognises that same vernacular adjective pattern directly and substitutes the formal Latin ending (-id -> -idae, -ine -> -inae, -oid -> -oidea) before ever falling back to fuzzy matching – an exact match on real data, not a guess. Two real examples from the name list, with the setting off vs. on:

    Original name Without consider_english_name_endings With it
    Staphylinine BF01 Staphylinidae sp. [...] (family – too broad) Staphylininae sp. [...] (subfamily – correct)
    Dermestid Indet. BF01 Dermestini sp. [...] (tribe – a coincidental, wrong fuzzy match) Dermestidae sp. [...] (family – correct)

    The second row matters as much as the first: without the exact-match check, broadest-first fuzzy matching had already found a real candidate for "Dermestid" (the tribe Dermestini) – just the wrong one. The ending substitution doesn’t just add precision, it can also correct a fuzzy match that was confidently wrong.

  • Hybrid, intergrade, indecision, and graded/“affinis” identifications all needed to resolve to genus rank only, since none of them can specify a genuine species – and the “affinis” case specifically needed to check for a real exact match first, for the tautonym reason above (issue #16).

The rules for aligning hybrids, intergrades, etc could be borrowed from APCalign’s function, as they were already carefully calibrated. However, a plant taxonomist’s reference list essentially never contains a subgenus bracket or the informal references to higher rank groupings the way an invertebrate collection’s does.

Swapping the reference: AFD + iNaturalist vs. AFD + GBIF

taxonAlign is designed to allow any taxonomic reference list to be used. To demonstrate this, the same 5,154-name list of invertebrate taxa was aligned a second time, this time against AFD combined with a GBIF-backbone-derived reference of Australian invertebrates, rather than reference lists from AFD + iNaturalist:

gbif_au <- readRDS("gbif_au_invertebrates.rds")
resources_gbif <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(list(AFD = afd, GBIF = gbif_au))

updated_gbif <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(
  old$original_name, resources_gbif,
  identifier = old$dataset_id,
  hybrids = TRUE, intergrades_affinis = TRUE, consider_english_name_endings = TRUE,
  include_bracketed_info = TRUE, progress = TRUE
)

The two combinations agree on 99.1% of all 5,154 names (98.5% on just the higher-rank subset, above). Where they disagree, it’s overwhelmingly explained by which resource happens to contain the specific name – good evidence that the reference and the matching engine really are two separable concerns, the way the package’s design intends.

Worth spelling out: since AFD is checked first in both combinations, every one of these disagreements is, by construction, a name AFD itself has no answer for – these are exactly the cases the AFD supplement was for, and iNaturalist and GBIF genuinely disagree about which of them they cover. A few real examples (leaving out the small number that turned out to be fuzzy-matching imprecision rather than a real coverage difference – that’s a limitation of taxonomic matching in general, not something this comparison is about):

Original name AFD + iNaturalist AFD + GBIF
Atalophlebioides sp. not resolved Atalophlebioides sp. [...] (genus)
Eurhopalus riguus not resolved Eurhopalus sp. [...] (genus)
Cardiodontulus BF01 Cardiodontulus sp. [...] (genus) not resolved
Scotocryptini spp. Scotocryptini sp. [...] (tribe) not resolved
Microsilpha BF01 Microscapha sp. [...] (genus, fuzzy-guessed) Microsilpha sp. [...] (genus, exact)

The last row is its own small lesson: iNaturalist doesn’t have the genus Microsilpha at all, so it fuzzy-matches to the coincidentally similar Microscapha instead – correctly resolving to genus rank by convention, but the wrong genus. GBIF happens to have the real name, so it matches it exactly. Same matching engine, same input name, different answer purely because of what each reference happens to contain.

The GBIF chapter

generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list() (now in taxonAlign.dataprep) is the one reference builder that doesn’t need a pre-existing export at all – it builds a reference directly from the live GBIF backbone taxonomy for any taxon:

gbif_reference <- taxonAlign.dataprep::generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list("Vanessa cardui")

Building a reference for every Australian invertebrate – the scale a full trait database actually needs – was a substantially harder engineering problem than fetching one small clade:

  • GBIF’s taxonomy-browsing API refuses to page past 100,000 rows into any single clade – a clade the size of Arthropoda (over three million descendants) has to be split recursively into smaller children and fetched piece by piece, with each piece cached independently as this became an oft-interrupted multi-day fetch.
  • A country filter can’t narrow the fetch itself – GBIF’s taxonomy-browsing endpoint has no country concept at all, only its occurrence-record endpoint does. The whole tree has to be fetched first and filtered to a country’s occurrences afterward.
  • Real network conditions at this scale – transient TLS failures, requests that hang rather than error – needed real retry-with-backoff and timeout handling, tuned against actual measured behaviour.

The result: a 358,496-row reference of Australian-occurring invertebrates, and a 3,987,219-row worldwide version built the same way without the country filter – confirming that a single worldwide dataset built once could serve any country’s alignment need, with the country filter applied locally and cheaply afterward.

The plan is to eventually deliver the gbif taxonomic dataset together with a function that will allow it to be further filtered by taxon group or country.

A faster route that turned up afterward

Most of the multi-day fetch above may not need repeating. The obvious shortcut, a ready-made copy of the GBIF backbone, was tried first: taxadb keeps one, and generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list() reads it. But in August 2026 taxadb’s copy turned out to be from December 2022, about four years old, and agreed with the live fetch on only 85% of names – not good enough to replace it.

While the live fetch was finishing, taxadb’s maintainer uploaded a current (2026) GBIF backbone snapshot to source.coop, as a single parquet file, before connecting it to the taxadb package itself (ropensci/taxadb#123). Against the live fetch, it agreed on about 99.9% of names. generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list()’s gbif_snapshot_url argument reads that file directly (issue #23):

# every animal in the 2026 GBIF backbone with an Australian occurrence record
gbif_au_animals <- taxonAlign.dataprep::generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list(
  "Animalia", rank = "kingdom", country = "AU",
  gbif_snapshot_url = "https://data.source.coop/cboettig/taxadb/2026/dwc_gbif_part_0.parquet",
  facet_limit = 3e5   # the default (1e5) is too small for all Australian animals (~220,000)
)

By the time the first data release was built (October 2026), this route existed, but the release’s GBIF_AU list was still built from the archived live fetch – the snapshot wasn’t considered. When GBIF_AU is next rebuilt, the snapshot should be the first option. It replaces only the slow part, fetching the taxonomy itself; two things stay the same:

  • The country filter still comes from GBIF’s occurrence records, via GBIF’s API, either way (that part is quick).
  • The snapshot has no extinct flag, so extinct taxa still need flagging separately, as for the current release (a name_lookup(isExtinct = TRUE) query per family took about five minutes for Australian vertebrates).

The maintainer hasn’t yet checked the snapshot against the taxadb package, and it’s a single undated “2026” file rather than a versioned release, so compare a snapshot-built list against the previous release before publishing one.

Lessons for whoever reads this next

  • A hand-built test fixture finds the bugs you anticipated; a real, large, messy dataset finds the ones you didn’t. Several of the real bugs referenced above were only found by running the full name list end to end and diffing the result against independent alignments or a real historical answer key – not by unit tests alone. The tests in tests/testthat/ exist to keep each fixed once found, not to have found them in the first place. AI does a fantastic job of building tests to catch the anticipated bugs, greatly reducing the time costs of writing tests for a new package. A well-versed human curator is (currently still) required to dig deeper and deeper into the match sequence to identify additional bugs. A long list of messy taxon names is the only way these bugs are uncovered.
  • A plausible-sounding fix deserves the same scepticism as the bug it’s fixing. The first attempt (by AI!) at fixing issue #16 was itself wrong, and only caught because a real, adversarial test (initiated by a human) (test-apc_equivalence.R) existed to catch it.
  • A reference built for one purpose tends to be useful for another. The GBIF reference built to validate this package against a real name list is, unmodified, also a candidate worldwide taxonomic resource in its own right.
  • Revisit a slow, hard-won approach when a faster one appears. The current GBIF snapshot (above) turned up partway through the project, but nobody went back to it when the first data release was built, so the release still used the old route.
